overview.title: Overview
overview.body:
This is development sample text, not approved destination information.

A destination story begins with an introduction: what visitors can discover and why the place matters. Approved content will appear here after editorial review.

Open another chapter to explore a different part of the story. Your reading size and position stay with this session.

history.title: History
history.body:
This is development sample text, not a historical account.

Origins
A researched chapter would introduce the origins of this place, with sources for every factual claim.

Change over time
Short paragraphs give each period room to breathe. Page controls let visitors read at their own pace while the panel stays in the scene.

People and memory
Community stories require permission, careful attribution and review. No names, dates or events in this sample describe a real destination.

notes.title: Visitor notes
notes.body:
Development layout sample. No real visitor rules, prices or opening hours are provided.

Before your visit
Reviewed access information belongs here. Changing details need a verification date.

While exploring
Keep pathways clear and pay attention to your surroundings when using the camera. Close the panel whenever you need an unobstructed view.

facts.title: Facts
facts.body:
Development sample only. These are content guidelines, not destination facts.

One idea at a time
A useful fact chapter explains a small number of interesting, verified details.

A reason to look closer
Approved copy can help visitors notice something meaningful. It must never imply that the camera recognizes an object.

Source before story
Unverified claims stay out of the published experience.

featuredResearch.title: Explore Ormoc in AR
featuredResearch.notice: Discover local stories, photographs and visitor tips.

D01.title: A living lake
D01.body: Forested slopes frame Lake Danao in the uplands of Ormoc, Leyte. Its long, curved outline is often compared with a guitar, while wooded headlands and ripples reward a closer look from shore. Arrive at the visitor entrance beside the viewing deck, rather than the broader park map pin. Enjoy sightseeing and picnics, or ask staff about kayaking, paddle boating, boat rides and floating-cottage rides. These activities share a landscape that also supports nearby fishing and farming communities. Check the day's activity arrangements before heading onto the water, and leave the shore as clean as you found it.

D01.title: Fish and everyday life
D01.body: Lake Danao's fish connect the water to local kitchens and livelihoods. Work with fishers in 2021–2022 recorded eight species by combining sampled catches with community knowledge; five species were collected directly. Families kept fish for meals, sold valuable catches and sometimes exchanged fish for other food. Preparations included tinola, a fish soup, and ginataan, cooked with coconut milk. These everyday choices reveal more than a list of species: they show how knowledge, food and income link people to the lake. As you look across the water, remember that this view is also part of someone's working landscape.

D01.title: A protected landscape
D01.body: Lake Danao and its surroundings became a protected natural park on 3 February 1998 and were included in the expanded national protected-area system in 2018. The lake and its habitats belong together; protecting the water also means caring for the land around it. Keep waste out of the lake and leave wildlife undisturbed. Take water safety seriously: this is deep water with a serious drowning risk. Swimming is permitted only inside the designated rope-lined area, never beyond it; the ropes do not guarantee safety. Follow staff instructions and wear a properly fitted life jacket for boating and floating-cottage rides.

D02.title: A lake framed by green
D02.body: Lake Kasudsuran is one of Ormoc's smaller upland lakes, in Barangay Ga-as. Ferns and tall shoreline grasses draw the eye toward open water, with wooded slopes rising beyond. Look from the plants along the bank to the reflections farther out: the close meeting of land and water gives the lake its character. Reaching this setting is a guided walk, not a drive to the lakeshore. Allow approximately one hour for the hike, agree the timing with your local guide, and leave enough daylight for the return. Take in the view from firm ground without trampling the shoreline vegetation.

D02.title: A working upland landscape
D02.body: Ga-as is a place of work as well as scenery. Its farmers grow cabbage, cassava and sweet potato, linking these uplands to city markets. Arrange a local guide, then begin at the road-end beside the basketball court in Sitio Maglahug. A guide is required, and access to the lake is on foot only. The small unpaved fork beyond the road-end is not a vehicle route or a shortcut through private property. Wear grippy trail shoes, carry water and rain protection, and follow your guide if rain or slippery ground changes the plan. Respect fields, homes and residents' paths.

D03.title: Within the green slopes
D03.body: Lake Janagdan rests among steep, green slopes in Barangay Cabintan, Ormoc, in the Mt. Aminduen area. A rocky waterline and reflections on a still surface bring the shape of the surrounding land into focus. Begin at Lake Janagdan Staging Area, not the lake's map pin, and hike with a required local guide. The uphill approach calls for care around roots, rocks and slippery ground, especially after rain. Wear grippy trail shoes, bring water and rain protection, and agree the day's route with your guide. At the lake, pause on firm ground and let the enclosed landscape reveal its details.

D03.title: A lake that matters to Cabintan
D03.body: Janagdan's story reaches beyond hiking. In 2018, a proposed access road faced opposition from mountaineers concerned about the mountain environment and the lake's role as a water source for Cabintan. The project was stopped, and reallocating remaining funds to other tourism roads was approved. This history helps explain why visiting also means caring for land and water shared with residents. Confirm local check-in arrangements before setting out, stay on the guide's route and allow enough daylight to return. Keep rubbish, soap and detergents out of the lake, leave plants undisturbed and ask your guide before considering any water activity.

D04.title: Where river, forest and bay meet
D04.body: At Naungan, the Pagsangaan River reaches Ormoc Bay beside mangrove forest and fishponds. Part of this coastal forest serves as a public park, bringing recreation into a landscape that supports local livelihoods. Mangroves shelter fish, crustaceans and other wildlife while helping stabilize the shore. Begin at the Naungan park entrance and explore only the paths open to visitors. Daylight makes it easier to appreciate the water, roots and shoreline; wear shoes with grip and take extra care on wet surfaces beside the water.

D04.title: A forest cared for by its community
D04.body: The Naungan–San Juan Mangrove Planters Association has worked with Ormoc’s local government and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to conserve and restore mangroves in Naungan, Lao and San Juan. A community forestry agreement in 2000 and an ecotourism initiative in 2017 mark stages in this work. Rehabilitation continued after Typhoon Haiyan damaged planted areas and nurseries. These efforts connect coastal livelihoods with environmental care. Respect that work by leaving roots, plants and wildlife undisturbed, keeping to open paths and carrying your litter away.

D05.title: Pineapple country
D05.body: Sal’s Pineapple Plantation sits beside Ormoc Diversion Road in Barangay Biliboy. The giant pineapple landmark marks the entrance and ride drop-off, making a memorable starting point for a visit. Visitors can walk inside the plantation while keeping clear of the crops. Beyond the view is a working agricultural landscape: pineapple growing supports livelihoods and helps shape Ormoc’s identity. The Queen variety is especially associated with the city, although it also grows elsewhere in Leyte and Eastern Visayas. See the fields as both a local landmark and a place of work.

D05.title: A fruit at the heart of the fiesta
D05.body: Queen pineapple is known for its sweetness, aroma and crisp texture, with fruit smaller than some other pineapple varieties. In Ormoc, it also has a cultural role. The Piña Festival brings pineapple imagery into street dancing, costumes and community celebrations during the city’s June fiesta season. The celebration honors the patron saints, Saints Peter and Paul, while giving local agriculture a place in public life. That connection helps explain why pineapple is such a recognizable city symbol. Here, a familiar fruit tells a larger story about growers, community pride and celebration.

D05.title: Walk gently through the growing fields
D05.body: The plantation route is popular locally for jogging and fun runs, but it remains a place where crops are growing. Walk on clear routes without stepping on plants or planted rows, and leave every pineapple intact. There is virtually no shade, so choose early morning or late afternoon; on a cooler evening, finish before dark. Bring drinking water, a hat and sun protection. Take photographs without entering the crops, keep access clear for workers and vehicles, and follow on-site instructions. Carry your litter away so the next visitor finds the fields just as inviting.

D06.title: Golf in Ormoc’s countryside
D06.body: Leyte Golf and Country Club is an 18-hole, par-72 course in Ormoc’s Mabini area. Its setting includes surrounding mountains and views toward Ormoc Bay, adding a sporting perspective to a city also known for lakes, farms and coastal scenery. For golfers, it offers a different way to experience the countryside. Arrange your visit with the club before travelling, including guest eligibility, booking and any playing requirements. The marked club location is also the registration area; check in there and follow staff directions before going farther onto the property.

D06.title: Trees, open ground and thoughtful play
D06.body: Spreading trees and open grass give the club’s landscape its character. The contrast between closely cut ground and branching canopies invites a slower look at the space around the game. Enjoy that setting from the areas staff authorize, without assuming the course is open for casual walks or sightseeing. Golf balls and moving carts make active playing areas unsuitable for unguided wandering. Wear suitable footwear, carry water and sun protection, and follow the club’s weather instructions. If thunder or lightning develops, stop outdoor activity and seek a substantial building as directed by staff.

D07.title: Above the folded ridges
D07.body: Alto Peak, also known as Mt. Aminduen, rises about 1,332 metres above sea level and is recognized as Eastern Visayas’ highest peak. Forested slopes and tightly folded ridges make the landscape feel larger than a single summit. The approach from Ormoc is associated with Cabintan, a community at the edge of this mountain country. Begin at the SULFATARA starting point rather than the summit map pin. Arrange a local guide before travelling; a guide is required. This is a strenuous mountain trek, not a beginner’s sightseeing stroll.

D07.title: Earn the view, respect the forest
D07.body: On Alto’s forest trails, the climb demands attention as well as stamina. Mud, slippery roots and steep ground can slow progress, and upper sections may involve scrambling and rope assistance. Wear grippy hiking footwear and bring rope-handling gloves, water, food, rain protection, a headlamp and first aid. Set the route, registration arrangements and turnaround time with your guide before setting out. Follow the guide’s instructions around ropes and steep sections; postpone or turn back when rain or conditions make the route unsafe. Stay on the agreed trail and carry out every piece of rubbish, leaving the forest intact.

D08.title: A garden beneath the mountains
D08.body: At Heaven’s Peak in Barangay Cabintan, the garden brings Ormoc’s upland scenery close enough to explore at walking pace. Flower borders, lawns and a stone path draw the eye toward the forested mountains beyond. Notice the change in scale: carefully tended plants are close at hand, while ridges form the backdrop. This is a garden viewpoint, not a summit trek. Arrive at the garden entrance and check opening and admission arrangements before travelling. Walk on the paths and give the planted borders room to flourish.

D08.title: Flowers in a working landscape
D08.body: Cabintan is more than a mountain backdrop: vegetable growing is part of the community’s livelihood. Seen in that setting, Heaven’s Peak offers another expression of people tending the uplands, this time through ornamental plants. Look from the flower beds toward the wider landscape and remember that homes and farms continue beyond the garden. Choose daylight and fair weather for enjoying the view; bring drinking water, sun or rain protection and shoes with a good grip. Paths can be slippery when wet. Keep children close, take your rubbish away and respect neighbouring homes and cultivated land.

D09.title: Hospitality beside Ormoc Bay
D09.body: Sabin Resort Hotel stands beside Ormoc Bay in Barangay Bantigue, where the waterfront gives the property its distinctive setting. Its story is tied to people coming together by the sea, first for simple recreation and later for hotel stays and gatherings. The bay remains the thread linking those different chapters. Arrive at the hotel entrance and check in with staff before exploring. Confirm your room, dining or visitor arrangements directly with the hotel before travelling, including which outdoor areas and facilities your visit allows you to use.

D09.title: From Sal’s Beach to a hotel
D09.body: Sabin’s story began with Sal’s Beach, a seaside recreation spot with simple bamboo-and-nipa huts. Visits from Ormoc and nearby towns encouraged Sabin A. Larrazabal to develop a larger property. In the hotel’s history, project planning began in 1990, followed by an expansion in 2006. From beach huts to accommodation and gathering spaces, the scale changed while the sea remained central. For a comfortable visit, bring sun or rain protection and suitable footwear.
